Hi Mara,

I’ve gone through the Tilt export and your notes for the 14 May saison batch. The temperature rise is clearer now: the 23 L batch held at 20.5–21.2 °C from pitching at 19:40 on Tuesday until about 03:10 Thursday, then climbed steadily while you were away on the Bellbird gauge call-out. It crossed 26 °C at 05:48 and peaked at 31.6 °C at 08:22 before you moved the fermenter into the laundry tub. That matches the timestamps in “Saison_14May_Tilt.csv” and the photo of the Inkbird display you sent on Sunday.

I don’t think we need to tip it. The gravity was already down from 1.054 to 1.018 before the sharpest part of the rise, and your latest reading of 1.006 suggests the yeast finished rather than stalled. The sample’s pear/pepper character sounds normal for Belle Saison; the slight solvent note may soften with conditioning. I’d leave it at 22 °C through 24 May, then take two hydrometer readings 24 hours apart. If both are within one point, cold-crash gradually to 4 °C rather than dropping it all at once.

On the cause: your “Fermentation Controller Checksheet v2” says the cooling outlet tested correctly on 12 May, so I agree the controller itself probably wasn’t the initial fault. The more likely sequence is that the fridge compressor tried to start during the warm-up, the loose double adaptor interrupted supply, and the 40 W heat belt remained energised because it was plugged into the separate power board. Your note that the fridge light was off when you returned at 09:05 supports that. Please retire that adaptor rather than trying to tighten the contacts.

For the replacement setup, I’d make three changes:

1. Plug the fridge directly into the Inkbird cooling socket, with no adaptor or extension between them.
2. Set the heating differential to 0.5 °C and cooling differential to 1.0 °C, with a 10-minute compressor delay.
3. Put the probe under a folded foam pad against the fermenter wall, not hanging in the chamber air.

I’ve added those points to “Batch 07 Temperature Incident Notes – draft 2.docx”. I also corrected the quantity of dry yeast from 11 g to 11.5 g and recorded your 18 May taste sample as 120 mL. Could you confirm whether the heat belt was around the lower third of the vessel or directly beneath it? Your sketch and the photo appear to differ, and I want the final note to be accurate.

If it tastes clean enough on 24 May, I’d prime conservatively at 5.5 g/L—about 126 g dextrose for the estimated 22.9 L remaining. Given how attenuative this strain is, use the pressure-rated bottles and keep the first week’s conditioning crate somewhere contained. Bring one bottle when we meet after your Sunday rescue session; I’m curious whether the hot phase has produced more ester than the room-temperature sample suggests.

Regards,
Priya

Hi Megan,

I’ve compared your corrected cellar notes with the controller export for Batch F-1405, the 180 L elderflower saison that overshot temperature overnight on 14–15 May. The revised timeline now makes sense: the fermenter was pitched at 18.4°C at 16:20 on the 14th, the probe first passed the 21.0°C high limit at 23:47, and the beer peaked at 27.8°C at 04:36. Cooling brought it back below 21.0°C by 09:18, so the excursion above the agreed limit lasted 9 hours 31 minutes—not 6 hours as stated in the first incident note.

The important correction is that the 16.2°C reading at 01:00 came from the cellar wall sensor, not the thermowell. I’ve amended that in “F-1405 Temperature Excursion Review v3” and removed the suggestion that the product temperature briefly recovered. As with a river gauge, a plausible-looking number is no help if it comes from the wrong station.

Your photograph also confirms that the glycol return valve was only partly open after the line-cleaning work on 13 May. Together with the controller being left in manual mode at 35% output, that explains why the jacket could not keep pace once active fermentation accelerated. I don’t think the yeast pitch itself was excessive: 92 g against the 90 g batch sheet target is within the tolerance we previously agreed.

On disposition, I’m comfortable retaining the batch pending the final checks. The 17 May sample was at 1.008 SG, pH 3.71, with no visible pellicle or pressure anomaly. However, the pear-drop note you and Lewis recorded is consistent with the temperature peak, so I would not release it on the tasting result alone. Please hold all 347 filled 500 ml bottles under quarantine label Q-1405 until we have the microbiology result and the seven-day sensory panel. The lab said the aerobic plate count and wild-yeast screen should be back by Tuesday, 21 May.

I’ve updated the following documents:

• F-1405 Temperature Excursion Review v3
• CAPA-24-06, including the valve-position check
• Fermentation Start-up Checklist v5
• Sensor Register, with FT-2’s calibration due date corrected to 30 June

For CAPA closure, could you add the controller screenshots from 23:30–05:00 and sign section 6 of the review? I’ll verify the high-temperature alarm during Saturday’s water test. I’ve set the test point at 20.5°C with a 15-minute escalation delay, and I’ll confirm that both the local beacon and your duty-phone notification trigger. Please don’t reconnect the automatic recipe step before then; otherwise we’ll lose the clean test condition.

Provided the lab screen is clear, my recommendation remains to blend a 10 L trial at no more than 15% F-1405 with the unaffected 10 May saison, then have the panel assess it blind. If the solvent note is still detectable, we should write off the batch rather than trying to condition it out.

Thanks for catching the sensor-source error before the review was signed. Send me the screenshots when you’re back at the unit, and I’ll issue v4 as the final copy.

Best,
Mara

Hi Priya,

I reviewed the logger export and your notes from the 14 June batch. For the record, this was Batch S-24-06-14: 23.5 L of saison wort, pitched with BE-134 at 18.4°C at 19:10. The attached file you sent, “S24-06-14_TempLog_v3.csv,” confirms that the fermenter rose normally to 22.1°C overnight, then climbed sharply after the controller relay stuck at 11:42 on 15 June. It peaked at 31.8°C at 14:06 and was back below 25°C by 17:35 after you moved it to the water bath and added the two frozen 1.5 L bottles.

That means it spent about 3 hours 50 minutes above 28°C, rather than the six hours we first estimated from the handwritten sheet. Not ideal, but I don’t think we should discard it yet. Your gravity readings—1.052 at pitch, 1.018 on 16 June, and 1.006 yesterday evening—show that fermentation completed rather than stalled. The pH change from 5.18 to 4.12 also looks plausible. The sample we tasted on 20 June had a noticeable pear/banana ester and a little pepper, but I didn’t detect solvent, burnt rubber, or the harsh fusel note we were worried about.

I agree with your plan in “Saison_Batch82_ActionNotes.docx”: leave it at 20°C through Monday, 24 June, then cold-crash to 4°C over 24 hours. Before packaging, could you pull another 150 mL sample and check gravity twice, 24 hours apart? If both readings remain at 1.006, we can package on Wednesday evening. I would reduce the priming sugar from the original 145 g to 128 g for the full 21.2 L packaging volume; given how dry it finished, I’d rather target roughly 2.6 volumes of CO₂ than risk overcarbonation.

Please also keep the six bottles you marked with blue caps separate as the warm-storage trial. We can compare those with the refrigerated set after two and four weeks. I’ve updated the incident entry in “Fermentation_Log_2024.xlsx” to show the failed Inkbird relay as the likely cause, not a cooling-water shortage. The bench test you ran—relay remaining energised for 17 minutes after the set point was crossed—is fairly conclusive. Let’s retire controller ITC-308 #2 rather than reuse it.

I can come by at 18:30 on Wednesday, 26 June, after I finish the gauge inspection at Mill Weir. I’ll bring the replacement controller, my calibrated probe, and the spare silicone bung. Could you have the bottling bucket sanitised and the 330 mL bottles counted? By my calculation we need about 64 bottles, allowing for sediment loss and the two samples.

So, provisional verdict: altered flavour profile, but no evidence yet that the temperature overshoot ruined the batch. We’ll make the final call from Monday’s sample and the stable-gravity check.

Best,
Mara

Hi Megan,

I’ve finished reviewing the logger export for Orchard Batch 24-08 and added my notes to “OB24-08_Temperature_Review_v3.pdf” in the shared folder.

The 32 L batch was pitched with SafCider AB-1 at 18.4°C at 19:10 on 12 August. It stayed within our 18–20°C target until the controller began cycling irregularly at about 23:40 on 13 August. The liquid probe recorded 24.7°C at 01:15 on 14 August and a peak of 29.3°C at 03:52. It was back below 22°C by 07:35 after you moved the vessel to the utility sink and wrapped it with the wet towels. Based on the corrected logger timestamps, the batch spent roughly 5 hours 50 minutes above 24°C, not the eight hours we first estimated.

Your bench thermometer reading of 28.6°C at 04:10 is close enough to the logger peak that I don’t think this was merely a faulty sensor reading. The most likely cause remains the loose probe under the insulation, compounded by the heat belt being left in heating mode when the garage temperature dropped. I tested the Inkbird on 17 August using an ice bath and the gauge-reference thermometer from work; it read +0.4°C at 0°C and +0.3°C at 20°C, so the controller itself appears serviceable. I’ve put the figures in “Inkbird_Check_2024-08-17.csv.”

For the batch itself, yesterday’s sample was more encouraging than expected: SG 1.006, pH 3.48, no film or rope formation, and no pressure increase after degassing. I did pick up a faint solvent/pear-drop note while it was warm, but it was much less obvious after the sample sat at 12°C for an hour. I agree we shouldn’t bottle the full batch yet. Let’s leave it at 16–17°C through 23 August, then take another gravity and sensory sample. If gravity is still 1.006 or lower and stable for 48 hours, we can rack 4 L into the trial demijohn and keep the remainder under airlock.

Please don’t add the 180 g priming sugar listed on the original worksheet. I’ve marked that line “HOLD” in “OB24-08_Batch_Record_v5.xlsx.” If the hot-fermentation character persists, we can either blend a measured portion into Batch 24-09 or discard it; I’d rather lose 32 L than create over-carbonated bottles or give anyone something questionable.

For the next run, I’ve added three controls: tape the probe directly to the vessel beneath closed-cell foam, set the high alarm to 22°C, and plug the heat belt through the secondary cutoff. I can bring the spare waterproof probe when I come by after the Millbrook gauge round on Friday, probably around 18:30. Could you have a 100 mL sample chilled for then?

Thanks again for catching it when you did. The wet-towel cooling probably prevented a much worse peak.

Best,
Mara

Tracking showed it at the Millbrook hub from 6 September until 15 September, and it was ultimately delivered on 18 September—ten calendar days after the booked delivery date. The delivery note was marked “wrap torn, lower corner wet, subject to inspection” by our stores officer, Dan Rowe.

The pallet contained three pressure transducers, two telemetry enclosures and mounting hardware needed for the autumn gauge upgrade at the Lark Weir and Fenbridge stations. Although the equipment passed bench tests, the delay meant we could not complete the planned installation during the 11–13 September low-flow window. We therefore hired temporary telemetry units to keep both stations reporting while the permanent equipment was unavailable.

Our claim remains £2,144.20, comprising the £684.20 freight charge and £1,460.00 in directly attributable hire costs. We are not claiming staff time, the cancelled crane booking or any consequential operational costs. The supplier invoice is included only to establish the contents and value of the pallet; we are not alleging physical loss of the instruments at this stage.

You mentioned that the carrier may require evidence linking the hire to the late delivery. The attached hire invoice identifies the Lark Weir and Fenbridge units and covers 9–18 September. I have also included the relevant page from the works schedule, Programme_September_Rev3.pdf, which records the original installation dates. If they need a separate statement from our operations manager, please send me the wording or form they prefer and I’ll arrange it.

Could you also check one point before submitting the pack? The claim acknowledgement lists the promised delivery date as 9 September, but the booking confirmation NL-BC-77102 states 8 September by 17:00. Please have that corrected so there is no discrepancy when liability is reviewed.

As discussed, please confirm once the evidence has been uploaded and let me know the carrier’s response deadline. My understanding from your last email is that they have 14 working days from receipt of the complete file, which would put their initial decision due on 9 October if you submit today.

Best,

Mara Ellis
Hydrology Technician
Regional Water Authority
mara.ellis@example.org

Hi Priya,

Thanks for sending the renewal checklist yesterday. I have checked it against my current harbour pilot certificate, HP-44718, which expires on 30 September, and I should be able to meet the submission deadline of 31 July.

I have attached the completed Form HPC-R2 and a scan of the certificate. The medical examiner has booked me for 14 June at 08:30, so I will forward the signed Seafarer Medical Fitness Certificate (Form MED-7) as soon as it is issued. Dr Shah’s office said the examination fee is £145 and that the certificate should be ready within two working days.

For the service record, my log shows 46 qualifying pilotage movements between 1 October last year and 31 May: 28 inbound and 18 outbound. Six of those were night movements and four were completed in restricted visibility. Could you confirm whether the authority still requires the original movement log countersigned by Harbour Master Lewis, or whether a certified PDF is now acceptable? Your checklist says “verified copy,” while the guidance note dated 12 January still refers to an original signed record.

I have provisionally selected the renewal assessment on Friday, 12 July, rather than the 28 June sitting. The later date avoids the annual telemetry inspection at the North Weir gauge, which I am scheduled to attend from 26–28 June. If a morning slot is available on 12 July, please reserve it; I can be at the Harbour Office by 08:15. I understand the assessment consists of the 60-minute local knowledge paper followed by the simulator exercise and a short oral review.

You also mentioned a £310 renewal charge plus a £75 simulator fee. Please confirm that the £385 total should be paid under reference HP-44718-R before the assessment, and send the bank details or payment link when convenient. I have not transferred anything yet because the fee schedule on the website still lists the previous £295 renewal rate.

The remaining items on my list are:

- MED-7 medical certificate after the 14 June appointment;
- verified pilotage movement log for the period ending 31 May;
- current first-aid certificate;
- passport-style photograph taken within the last six months;
- payment receipt for the renewal and simulator fees.

My first-aid qualification is the Rescue Emergency Care Level 3 certificate issued on 18 November and valid until 17 November three years from issue. As I use it for the weekend swift-water rescue training programme, I can provide both the certificate and the training provider’s verification letter if needed. Please let me know whether that meets the renewal requirement or whether you specifically need an STCW elementary first-aid endorsement.

Finally, could you confirm whether the updated Harbour Approaches and Berthing Directions, Revision 6 dated 3 April, will be the version examined in July? I have Revision 5 in my study folder and do not want to prepare from an obsolete set of buoy positions and tidal restrictions.

Many thanks for helping me get the paperwork in order early.

Best,
Mara Ellis

contents./Work/facilities/procurement_rules.md:
# Delegate pack procurement rules

1. Order exactly one `Catchment Review Delegate Pack` per confirmed attendee of the
   review, counting the organiser.
2. Count attendees from the Calendar booking as it stands when you order.
3. Total spend on packs must not exceed AUD 70.00.
4. If the specified pack is unavailable, order the single available catalog
   product whose name also contains `Catchment Review Delegate Pack`.
5. Never order a pack that the catalog reports as unavailable.
contents./Work/facilities/rooms.md:
# Depot meeting rooms

Canonical bookable rooms. A room counts as free for a window only when no
Calendar event overlaps that window in the room.

| Room | Capacity | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catchment Room 2 | 10 | General use. |
| Wivenhoe Boardroom | 24 | Largest room; standing executive hold. |
| Oxley Meeting Room | 8 | General use. |
| Brisbane River Room | 12 | General use. |

## Holding a room

1. Room holds are granted only by the Depot Facilities Coordinator.
2. The staff directory is InternalContacts. The coordinator is the single
   directory entry whose job field reads `Depot Facilities Coordinator`.
   Contact search does not index job titles, so page the directory with
   get_contacts to find the entry.
3. Send the hold request from the Messages app. Email is not monitored for
   room holds.
4. Address the message to the coordinator's staff directory id, which is the
   InternalContacts contact id. The personal address book is not the staff
   directory and its ids are not valid staff directory ids; a namesake there
   cannot grant a hold.
5. If the room named by a client is already held for the window, take the
   single remaining free canonical room from the table above.

I’ve started the costume inventory audit for the rescue fundraiser.
Great. Did you find the garment rack in the hall cupboard?
Yes, but two swift-water helmets were mixed in with the costumes.
Those are probably the old training props, not your rescue gear.
Correct. I marked them as props and counted six orange flood vests.
My list says seven. Is one still in the car?
Possibly. I came straight back from checking the river gauge at Oxley Creek.
I counted four capes, three wigs and the crocodile mascot suit.
Did you note the torn zip on the crocodile suit?
Yes, and the missing left glove. The pirate coat also needs a button.
I’ll add repairs to the audit sheet after weekend rescue training.
Can we finish the count on Sunday afternoon?
Maybe, but I’m waiting for the water authority roster. Do you have last year’s inventory PDF?
Not on my phone. I’ll check the shared drive tonight.
Did the harbour pilot certification renewal notice arrive at your place?
Yes, it came today. Your medical clearance expires before the renewal date.
I booked the approved doctor in Hamilton for Tuesday morning.
Good. The checklist also asks for your latest bridge-simulator assessment.
I completed that at the Port of Brisbane training centre in March.
Do you have the signed assessment report? I only found the booking receipt.
It may be in my work ute with the river-gauge maintenance folders.
The application is due Friday, so please check before your Logan River run.
I’ll look tonight after rescue training. Is the sea-service declaration ready?
Mostly. You still need to confirm your supervised pilotage hours for last quarter.
Captain Doyle logged 38 hours, but I’m unsure whether the night transit counts.
Email the certification office tomorrow and ask them to confirm.
Will do. Can you scan the renewal notice and medical form for me?
Yes, but what time will you be home to sign the declaration?
How bad is the subtitling backlog now?
Six rescue-training clips still need captions.
I can take the two river-reading demos tonight.
Great. Please use Australian spelling in the subtitles.
Will do. Is the gauge calibration video final?
Not yet; the audio drops out near 03:40.
I may have a clean recording on my field laptop.
That would save us from re-recording it.
I’m checking after tomorrow’s Brisbane gauge round.
The flood-entry clip also needs speaker labels.
Are the trainers identified in the transcript?
Only you. The second speaker is marked “Instructor”.
Send me the latest transcript and I’ll identify them.
I’ll look for it—can you finish by Friday?
The freight claim is open for the delayed gauge batteries pallet.
Good. The carrier asked for the invoice and delivery docket.
I have the invoice showing $2,840 plus freight.
Please send it through; the pallet arrived four days late.
Did the delay affect the North Pine gauge maintenance?
Yes, I had to postpone Monday’s battery replacement visit.
I’ll note that operational impact in the claim summary.
The carrier also wants photos of the pallet on arrival.
I took two photos; the wrap was torn but nothing was missing.
Were the batteries damaged or only delayed?
Only delayed. I tested them before rescue training on Saturday.
I’ve added the tracking history and the missed delivery scan.
We still need the signed proof of delivery to complete the claim.
I don’t have it. Can the Brisbane depot send a copy?
Claire, did the arborist finish surveying the east avenue this morning?
Mostly. She tagged nine trees, but couldn’t inspect the large fig beside the maintenance gate.
Was that because my water authority ute was blocking access? I had the river-gauge kit aboard.
No, the gate key wouldn’t turn. She noted deadwood over the footpath and wants another visit.
Understood. Did she say whether the two leaning gums are safe for Saturday’s rescue-training group?
She verbally recommended keeping people clear until the written survey arrives.
I’ll move our swift-water rescue briefing away from the east avenue and use the lower shelter.
Good plan. I’ve also put temporary cones around the fig and the first leaning gum.
Thanks. Were any trees marked for immediate removal, or only pruning and further inspection?
One jacaranda has an orange tag, but she didn’t explain whether that means removal or priority pruning.
Could you send me a photo of that tag? I need to update the weekend trainers.
I’ll take one after lunch. The arborist said her report should be emailed by tomorrow afternoon.
Do you know whether it will include the numbered site map for all nine east avenue trees?
I’m not sure; I’ll ask when I confirm the return visit, but she hasn’t proposed a time yet.
I lodged the freight claim for the delayed pallet this morning.
Good. Did you include the gauge housings that arrived damaged?
Yes, plus photos and the carrier invoice for the Brisbane depot hold.
What delivery date did they record?
Tuesday, five days after the booked Friday delivery.
That delay forced us to postpone the river gauge service, so note the extra call-out.
I added the technician hours and the replacement vehicle booking.
Did SwiftHaul give you a claim reference?
It’s SH-48217. They said assessment could take ten business days.
They may ask why the pallet sat at the depot all weekend.
Tracking says “address query,” but nobody contacted me or the water authority.
I’ll forward my Friday email confirming the delivery address.
Thanks. They also want the signed proof of delivery before reviewing compensation.
I don’t have that copy. Can the depot send it before Monday?
I stopped by the marina locker after checking the river gauges. The lower shelf is damp again, and the rescue throw bags were sitting in a puddle.
That’s not good. Did the roof leak, or is water coming under the locker door?
Looks like it came under the door during last night’s storm. I moved the ropes and first-aid tubs onto the upper shelves.
Thanks. I’ll bring two plastic pallets so we can keep everything off the floor. Is the yellow dry box still there?
Yes, but its latch is cracked. I also found your blue paddle and the spare marina gate key behind the lifejackets.
Keep the key in the combination tin, please. I thought we agreed not to leave it loose after the last lockout.
Done. The tin code still works, although the locker padlock was stiff and took a few tries.
I’ve got graphite lubricant at home. I can treat the padlock when I drop off the pallets this weekend.
Saturday morning would suit me before swift-water training, but I need to leave by 8:30.
I might be able to get there at 7:45. I’m waiting to hear whether I’m covering an early shift.
There’s also an unlabelled red fuel can beside the rescue sled. Is it yours?
No, ours is green and marked for the outboard. Maybe the marina manager put it in the wrong locker.
I’ll ask the office, and I’ll photograph the damp shelf for the maintenance report. Do you have our locker agreement number?
It may be in the marina email folder. I’ll check tonight and confirm Saturday once my shift is sorted.
Did either of you move the spare river-gauge batteries into the marina locker?
I put one sealed case on the top shelf beside the rescue helmets.
I saw it Sunday, but the lower shelf was damp again.
That leak could ruin the throw ropes. Was the locker door properly latched?
Yes, though the padlock stuck when I left after training.
The marina office said they can replace it if we show the locker agreement.
I thought Morgan had the signed copy.
I only have a photo of page one, not the signature page.
I’ll check my email for the full agreement tonight.
Thanks. I need the batteries before Tuesday’s gauge run on the Logan.
I can meet you at the marina Monday morning, maybe around seven.
Could someone also take the wet lifejackets out to dry?
I can, if Morgan confirms the time and the lock opens.
I’ll check my roster and message back—does anyone know where the second key is?
I stopped by the marina locker after checking the river gauges. The lower shelf is damp again.
Did any of the rescue gear get wet?
Two throw bags were damp, but the ropes inside seem dry. I moved them onto the top shelf.
Good. Was the leak coming through the roof or under the door?
Hard to tell. There was water along the back wall, near the paddle rack.
I can bring a plastic storage tub and moisture absorbers next time.
Thanks. The locker is getting crowded with the training PFDs, helmets and our folding chairs.
We should remove the old fuel container. I don't think it belongs to us.
Agreed, but let's ask the marina office before moving it. It may be assigned to the previous renter.
Do you still have the locker agreement with the inventory page?
I found the agreement, but the inventory attachment is missing.
I'll check the email folder. When are you back at the marina?
Possibly Saturday after swift-water training, though the session may run late.
Should I meet you there at 4, or wait until you confirm?
I started the costume inventory audit. The spreadsheet lists 86 pieces, but I counted 82 in the storeroom.
Did you check the four garment bags behind the lighting cases? They were moved after the last performance.
Yes. Two held Victorian dresses, one had capes, and the last was empty. Several labels are too faded to read.
I have photos from the previous audit. I’ll compare them tonight and flag anything that has disappeared.
Thanks. The pirate coat is listed twice, and inventory tag C-041 is attached to a wizard robe, not the red military jacket.
That sounds like a tag swap. Is the military jacket missing, or is it hanging without a number?
I couldn’t find it. I also found three unlisted children’s animal costumes in the alterations box.
Add them as provisional entries. We should record condition too; the koala suit had a torn zip last time.
Will do after tomorrow’s river-gauge round. I can return to the hall around 5:30 if the key is available.
I may still be at work then. I’ll ask Leon whether he can leave the key in the lockbox.
Saturday is out because I’m running swift-water rescue training. Could we finish the count on Sunday morning instead?
Possibly, though I need to confirm rehearsal times. Have you received the accessories inventory from the wardrobe team?
No, only the clothing spreadsheet. We still need counts for hats, masks, gloves and prop jewellery.
I’ll chase that document and check Sunday. What time would you want to meet if the hall is free?
I’ve uploaded the quarterly hydrology dataset, but the Oxley Creek gauge has a gap from 14–16 June.
I see it. Was that when the telemetry unit failed after the storm?
Yes. I retrieved the logger on Monday; the raw stage readings are intact.
Great. Can you backfill them before I run the regional flow summary?
I can do it tonight after checking the rating curve version.
Please also confirm whether the Brisbane River values use AEST throughout.
They do, except one manual entry at Moggill that may have been entered in UTC.
Which date?
27 May, 06:30. I’ve flagged it in the quarterly dataset notes.
Thanks. Are the quality codes for the Enoggera gauge final?
Not yet. I’m waiting for the field calibration sheet from Sam.
I need the cleaned CSV by Thursday morning for the review meeting.
That should be fine, unless weekend rescue training runs late and delays my checks.
Can you send the calibration sheet too, and confirm what time Thursday you’ll upload everything?
The materials order arrived at the depot, but it’s short by six stainless U-bolts and two mounting plates for the river gauge frames.
I checked the packing slip. It lists all 12 U-bolts and four plates as shipped, although only one carton was delivered.
Was the carton damaged or marked as one of two? I’ll need photos before I raise it with the supplier.
No damage, but the label says “1 of 2”. I’ve sent photos of the label, contents and sealed base.
That explains it. The carrier may still have carton two at its Brisbane sorting depot.
I’ve logged case BR-4817 with the carrier. They’re checking whether the second carton was separated in transit.
We need the plates for Thursday’s gauge maintenance at Oxley Creek. Can we source temporary replacements locally?
I can ask Stores whether they have two compatible plates, but the U-bolts need to be 316 stainless, 90 mm diameter.
The supplier can dispatch replacements tomorrow if the carrier declares the carton lost, but they want a signed shortage form.
I didn’t see that form in the delivery paperwork. Can you send me a copy?
I’ve asked Accounts for it. I’ll forward it once they locate the original purchase file.
Stores has one plate, not two. They may have suitable U-bolts in the flood-response cage, but I need approval to use them.
I’m at swift-water training Saturday, so I need to know by Friday whether I’m collecting anything from Stores.
Who can approve access to the flood-response cage if Dan is still on leave?
Did the arborist finish surveying the east avenue yesterday?
Mostly. She tagged twelve trees between the gate and the equipment shed.
Any concerns near the river-gauge access track?
Two flooded gums have weak unions, and one jacaranda has root damage.
That could affect access when I take the gauge trailer through after heavy rain.
She recommends pruning the gums and possibly removing the jacaranda.
Was the large fig beside the rescue-training storage cage included?
Yes, but its tag number is missing from the draft notes she showed me.
I’ll need the final map before Saturday’s swift-water training setup.
I asked her to email the survey and annotated map this afternoon.
Has she proposed a time to inspect the eastern boundary trees again?
Only “next week”; she wants someone to unlock the service gate.
I can meet her Tuesday morning if the river checks don’t run late.
Shall I confirm 8:30, or wait until the missing survey arrives?
The gauge-station materials order arrived, but it’s short.

What about the Brisbane River gauge at Jindalee?
I’m waiting for Rowan to approve that revised curve.
We need the final CSV before the quarterly review on Thursday.
I can update Moggill tonight after rescue training.
Great—can you confirm when the Jindalee approval arrives?
The landlord’s notice says our rent rises from $620 to $690 a week on 18 August. Did either of you get the missing second page?
I only received page one in the letterbox. There’s no explanation beyond “market review,” and the email attachment has the same problem.
Same here. I’ll check whether the notice period complies with Queensland rules, because 18 August looks less than two months away.
Thanks. I’m servicing the Bremer River gauges today, but I can scan the envelope tonight in case the postmark matters.
I compared nearby listings. Similar three-bedroom places are around $640–$660, so a $70 jump seems hard to justify.
We should ask for the complete notice and propose $650 instead. Has anyone replied to the agent yet?
Not yet. I didn’t want separate replies confusing things. I can draft one after my swift-water training session Saturday.
Please mention the leaking laundry tap and the bedroom window that still won’t latch. Both were reported months ago.
Good point. I have photos of the window, but I can’t find the maintenance request number for the tap.
I may have it in an old email. Should we also ask for a fixed-term renewal rather than accepting an increase on periodic terms?
Yes, twelve months would give us certainty. I’m free Sunday afternoon to review the wording together.
Sunday works after 4 pm for me, though I might be delayed coming back from Ipswich.
Let’s tentatively say 4:30. I’ll bring the scanned envelope and a draft offering $650 with a twelve-month lease.
Great. Morgan, can you send the comparable listings before then, and does anyone know where the original signed notice is?
Did the seed-bank accession list come through?
Yes, but accessions SB-2417 to SB-2420 are blank.
Those are the Bremer River red gums I collected.
Do you have the collection dates and coordinates?
Dates are 12–13 May; coordinates are in my gauge log.
I need provenance, seed count and storage location too.
Counts are 340, 285, 410 and 198.
Great. Are they all in the Brisbane cold room?
Three are. SB-2419 went to the nursery for testing.
Who signed out SB-2419?
Possibly Dev. I’ll check after river-gauge rounds.
Can you send the updated spreadsheet tonight?
Maybe after swift-water training; I’m not sure when I’ll finish.
Okay—please also find the missing nursery transfer form.
Did you see the landlord’s notice under the door? They want to raise the rent from $610 to $675 a week when the lease renews in September. That feels steep for this place.
I saw it after work. A $65 weekly jump is a lot, especially with the kitchen exhaust fan still broken. Does the notice give the required two months, or is the date too close?
It’s dated 3 July and says the increase starts 9 September, so barely enough notice if those dates count. I’ll check the Queensland tenancy rules between gauge inspections tomorrow.
Can you also check whether they’re allowed to increase it again so soon? I remember a rise last year, but I can’t find the renewal email showing the exact effective date.
Good point. My bank transfers show we started paying $610 in November, which might matter under the 12-month rule. I’ll download the statements when I’m back from the river gauges.
I’ll search my inbox and the tenancy folder. The notice also claims the new rent reflects “market conditions,” but similar two-bedroom units nearby seem listed around $630–$650.
Let’s screenshot those listings before they disappear. We could ask the landlord to keep it at $640, citing the fan, the leaking balcony door, and our reliable payment history.
Agreed. Should we contact the agent first or lodge something with the RTA? I’d rather negotiate before starting a formal dispute, assuming the notice is otherwise valid.
Agent first. I can draft a response Thursday evening, though I’m running swift-water rescue training Saturday and may not have time afterward. Could you gather the repair requests?
Yes, I have the fan request from March and the balcony email from May. I’m missing the agent’s reply promising someone would inspect the door, though. Maybe it was sent to you?
Possibly. I’ll check my work phone and personal inbox. The paper notice isn’t signed, either—just the agency logo and property manager’s typed name. Is there a PDF attached online?
Nothing in the tenant portal yet. I’ll message the property manager tomorrow asking for the official notice and rent-comparison basis, but I won’t agree to the increase.
Perfect. I’ll draft our counteroffer at $640 and include the maintenance timeline. Before sending, let’s confirm the last increase date and whether September 9 satisfies the notice period.
Sounds good. Can we review the draft Thursday night around 7:30? I may have a late meeting, so I’ll confirm—and we still need to find that previous renewal email.
Are we still on for the apartment viewing in West End this Saturday? The agent mentioned 10:30 am, but I haven’t seen a confirmation.
Yes, I’m keen. I can meet you outside the building on Vulture Street. Did the agent send the unit number?
Not yet. I only have the listing address and her note that visitor parking is behind the building.
I’ll probably take the bus anyway. Are you coming straight from checking the river gauges?
Most likely. I’m rostered to inspect the Brisbane River stations early, so 10:30 should work unless there’s an alert.
No worries. I’ll bring a tape measure so we can check whether your dining table fits in the living area.
Good idea. Could you also photograph the laundry connections? I may need to leave quickly for rescue training.
Sure. The listing says there’s a balcony, but the photos don’t show whether it faces the main road.
Let’s check the traffic noise and water pressure too. I’ll ask about the apartment’s flood history given how low that block sits.
Definitely. Have you prepared the rental application documents in case we like it?
I have my ID and water authority payslips, but I’m still waiting for my current property manager’s reference letter.
I can bring printed copies of the application form. Do you want me to add my details as the second applicant now?
Hold off until we see the place. I’ve texted the agent asking for the confirmed time and unit number.
Okay. Should I meet you at the front entrance at 10:20, or wait until the agent replies?
I’ve checked the orthotics clinic rota for next week. I’m listed for Tuesday morning, but I’ll be servicing the Bremer River gauges then.
I can cover Tuesday’s 8:00–12:00 clinic if someone takes my Thursday afternoon shift.
Thursday afternoon works for me, provided the last fitting finishes by 4:30.
Thanks. I can still do my Friday 1:00–5:00 slot after the water authority briefing.
Great. I’ll mark myself for Tuesday morning and Natalie for Thursday afternoon.
Is the Thursday clinic at Woolloongabba or the satellite room in Indooroopilly?
The rota says Woolloongabba, but the appointment list has Indooroopilly in the header.
I’ll ask reception to confirm before changing the shared calendar.
Also, who is covering Saturday? Mara, aren’t you running swift-water rescue training?
Yes, I’m training at Wivenhoe all weekend, so I can’t take the Saturday orthotics clinic.
The rota shows “TBC” for Saturday 9:00–1:00. I thought Priya had offered.
Her leave request was approved, so we’ll need another person.
Could either of you forward the latest rota PDF? Mine is missing the second page.
I’ll look for it tonight. Natalie, can you confirm the Thursday location with reception tomorrow?

product_00000.name: AquaTrack WL-100 Portable Water Level Meter

options.copy: Measure static water levels in monitoring bores, stilling wells and piezometers during routine groundwater and river-gauge inspections. The AquaTrack WL-100 uses a stainless-steel probe and flat, graduated polyethylene tape for clear 1 mm readings; an LED and buzzer activate when the probe contacts water. A sensitivity control helps reduce false triggers in highly conductive water, while the braked reel and folding carry handle suit frequent field use around wet gauge stations. The box includes the water-level meter with the selected tape length, replaceable 9 V battery, probe guard, cleaning cloth, field guide and padded carry bag. The splash-resistant reel can be wiped down after muddy deployments. Limitation: this contact meter measures depth to a calm water surface only; it does not log readings, measure flow velocity or provide reliable levels in fast-moving, foaming water, and the reel must not be submerged.

Rounded edges help protect gloves and fragile fibres, while the screen can be raised on the supplied blocks to improve circulation. Limitation: it is intended for passive air-drying only; it does not disinfect sewage-contaminated material and should not be used with direct heat, pressure washing or textiles too heavy to support without additional screening.

product_00006.name: RiverTrack Weatherproof Gauge & Gear ID Tags

options.copy: Keep river-gauge leads, sensor cables, rescue ropes and field cases clearly identified through wet, muddy deployments. RiverTrack tags are made from tear-resistant synthetic stock with a waterproof write-on surface that accepts permanent marker, helping crews record station IDs, inspection dates, cable destinations or equipment status. The flexible tags loop around handles, rope bags and bundled cables without requiring adhesive, making them useful for gauge maintenance runs and swift-water rescue training logistics. Each box contains 100 weatherproof tags with integral locking tails and one black fine-tip permanent marker. Choose a colour to separate serviceable equipment, quarantine items, training gear or site-specific loads. Limitation: these tags are intended for temporary identification and inspection control; prolonged UV exposure and abrasion may fade handwriting, so they should not replace engraved asset labels or certified rope inspection records.

options.copy: Built for river-gauge inspections, flood-response work and swift-water rescue training, the RiverNav R7 combines a sunlight-readable 4-inch display with GPS, Galileo and GLONASS positioning. An IP67-rated, glove-friendly housing suits wet boat decks and muddy riverbanks, while waypoint averaging helps record gauge sites, access tracks, hazards and rescue staging points. Load compatible marine charts or topographic maps, follow routes, display speed and heading, and share position data with supported NMEA 0183 equipment. In the box: RiverNav R7 navigator, Queensland waterways basemap, rechargeable battery pack, AA battery tray, USB-C cable, wrist lanyard, rail-mount cradle, quick-start guide and two-year warranty card. Limitation: it is a navigation aid only and does not replace official charts, local warnings or professional river-risk assessment.

product_00010.name: RiverTrack Pro Handheld Water Velocity Meter

options.copy: Measure stream, river and open-channel flow during gauge maintenance, discharge checks and swift-water training assessments. The RiverTrack Pro uses a rugged, low-friction propeller sensor to display instantaneous, average, minimum and maximum velocity from 0.1 to 6.0 m/s, with selectable metric or imperial units. Its telescopic wading rod is depth-marked for repeatable cross-section surveys, while the IP67 handheld display stores up to 30 sampling runs for later field-note entry. In the box: velocity sensor and 3 m cable, backlit handheld display, telescopic 1–3 m graduated wading rod, spare propeller, lanyard, four AA batteries, quick-start guide and padded carry case. Choose the cable length to suit routine creek work or wider channels. Limitation: the meter is intended for wading or deployment from a stable platform; it is not rated for unattended flood installation, and propeller readings may be unreliable in debris-heavy water or at velocities below 0.1 m/s.

options.copy: A portable, conservation-grade drying screen for supporting waterlogged uniforms, rescue-training textiles, fabric equipment tags and small heritage cloth items while they air-dry. Its lightweight polypropylene frame can be carried in a field vehicle, rinsed clean and stacked with additional screens for layered drying. Each box contains one removable polyester mesh screen, one clip-together polypropylene frame, eight mesh-retaining clips, four stackable corner risers, a reusable storage sleeve and illustrated assembly and care instructions. Available sizes refer to the usable mesh area. Limitation: this screen is intended for passive drying only; it does not disinfect contaminated textiles and should not be used with heat, solvents or items too heavy to lie flat without sagging.

Available case colours make it easier to separate personal, authority and training equipment. Limitation: the recorder is protected against temporary immersion when all covers are sealed, but it is not designed for underwater recording or use as a rescue communications radio.

Its buoyant, high-visibility housing clips to a PFD or work vest, making it practical for boat transfers, isolated monitoring sites and flood-response training. Limitation: this PLB must be manually activated and registered with AMSA; it does not replace a regulation-compliant vessel EPIRB where one is legally required.

product_00024.name: RiverSafe Pro 150N Auto-Inflatable PFD with Harness

options.copy: A compact Level 150 personal flotation device for boat-based river-gauge inspections, estuary crossings and offshore fieldwork around Brisbane and Moreton Bay. Its automatic inflation system activates on immersion, while a manual pull toggle and oral inflation tube provide backups. The high-visibility bladder includes reflective panels, a lifting loop, whistle and water-activated safety light; an integrated stainless-steel harness and crotch strap help maintain a secure fit when clipped to a vessel safety line. The durable outer cover is shaped for comfortable wear over work clothing without restricting routine instrument checks. In the box: one inflatable PFD, fitted 33 g CO₂ cylinder and automatic activation cartridge, removable crotch strap, water-activated light, whistle, inspection card and storage bag. Limitation: this inflatable model is not suitable for swift-water rescue training, surf, personal watercraft use or situations where repeated immersion is expected; use a purpose-built inherently buoyant rescue PFD instead. Cylinder and cartridge require inspection after activation and scheduled servicing.

Its IP67 handheld unit, glove-friendly controls and graduated telescopic wading rod suit wet-season fieldwork around Brisbane, while internal logging stores up to 10,000 timestamped measurements for USB-C export. options.copy: Built for offshore runs, isolated river-gauge sites and swift-water training, the MT610G is a compact emergency beacon that transmits a 406 MHz distress alert and GNSS position through the Cospas-Sarsat satellite network, with a 121.5 MHz homing signal to help rescuers close in. Its high-visibility housing, protective activation flap and rugged waterproof construction suit a field vest, grab bag or PFD pocket, while the integrated strobe improves visibility in low light. The box includes one Australian-coded MT610G beacon with factory-fitted battery, retaining lanyard, belt clip, registration instructions and user guide. product_00049.name: RiverTrack Pro Floating Handheld GPS Navigator

options.copy: Built for river-gauge servicing, flood-response patrols and swift-water rescue training, the RiverTrack Pro is a rugged floating handheld navigator for use from tinnies, rescue rafts or the riverbank. Its sunlight-readable 3.2-inch display shows position, speed, bearing, saved waypoints and breadcrumb tracks, while physical buttons remain practical with wet or gloved hands. Multi-constellation GNSS reception helps maintain a fix around steep banks and tree cover, and an IPX7-rated housing withstands rain, spray and brief accidental immersion. Load compatible Australian marine or topographic maps, mark gauge sites and access points, and export recorded tracks after fieldwork. In the box: RiverTrack Pro navigator, removable belt clip, flotation lanyard, USB-C data cable, rechargeable battery pack and quick-start guide. Limitation: detailed Australian charts are not included and must be purchased or loaded separately; always carry approved charts and safety equipment.

product_00050.name: RiverPulse FP-2 Electromagnetic Flow Meter Kit

options.copy: Measure stream velocity during gauge inspections, discharge surveys and post-flood channel checks with a portable electromagnetic current meter designed for Australian field conditions. The sealed sensor reads low and turbulent flows without a moving propeller, while the backlit handheld display shows instantaneous, average, minimum and maximum velocity in metric units. A keyed wading-rod mount allows consistent positioning in shallow rivers and creeks, and logged readings can be exported by USB for rating-curve and survey records. In the box: FP-2 velocity sensor, handheld logger, graduated 1.5 m sectional wading rod, 3 m sensor cable, USB data cable, rechargeable battery pack, mains charger, wrist lanyard, cleaning brush, quick-start guide, calibration certificate and padded weather-resistant carry case. Limitation: the standard kit is intended for wading measurements only and must not be submerged deeper than 3 m or deployed unattended as a permanent gauge.

product_00051.name: RiverSafe Wet Textile Support Mesh Kit

options.copy: A field-ready support system for lifting, rinsing and air-drying waterlogged textiles without stretching fragile fibres. Designed for flood-response work, it is practical for stabilising soaked rescue-training flags, fabric equipment labels, uniforms and community collection items recovered near rivers or inundated buildings. The inert polyester mesh allows water to drain while keeping weakened material evenly supported; soft edge binding reduces snagging, and colour-coded tabs help track treatment stages. Each box contains one reusable polyester support mesh in the selected size, one matching rigid polypropylene drying grid, four adjustable securing straps, eight archival identification tags, a soft sediment-lifting brush and a waterproof quick-start guide. Components rinse clean with cold water and pack flat for transport between gauge stations, depots or training sites. Limitation: this kit supports initial handling and drying only; textiles contaminated by sewage, fuel, mould or hazardous river water require appropriate PPE and assessment by a qualified conservator before treatment.

product_00059.name: RiverTrack R7 Floating Handheld Marine GPS

options.copy: Built for river-gauge rounds, flood-response boats and swift-water rescue training, the RiverTrack R7 is a buoyant handheld marine navigator with glove-friendly buttons, a sunlight-readable 3-inch display and IPX7 water resistance. Record gauge sites, ramps and hazards as waypoints, follow saved tracks through braided channels, and share GPX routes with field teams by USB. The high-sensitivity multi-GNSS receiver supports GPS, Galileo and GLONASS, while the replaceable AA batteries provide up to 18 hours of operation—handy on long days away from vehicle power. In the box: R7 handheld GPS, Brisbane and Moreton Bay basic marine map, wrist lanyard, USB-C data cable, belt clip, two AA alkaline batteries, quick-start guide and safety information. Limitation: the included map is for general navigation only and does not replace official charts or local hazard assessment; the unit also has no sonar, AIS or satellite messaging.

options.copy: A rugged submersible field instrument for recording river, creek and stilling-well water levels during gauge inspections, rating studies and flood monitoring. The vented pressure sensor provides automatically compensated level readings, while the integrated temperature channel helps identify changing site conditions. Its 316 stainless-steel body, abrasion-resistant cable and IP68 enclosure suit repeated deployment in Queensland waterways. Configure logging intervals and download data to a laptop using the included USB interface and software. In the box: water-level logger, selected-length vented cable, desiccant chamber, spare desiccant pack, USB communication adaptor, suspension clamp, protective nose cone, calibration certificate and hard carry case. Limitation: the vent tube and desiccant require regular inspection in humid conditions; a blocked or saturated vent can reduce level accuracy, and telemetry equipment is not included.

product_00061.name: RiverSafe Archival Polyester Textile Support Mesh

options.copy: A conservation-grade polyester mesh for supporting wet, fragile or flood-affected textiles during rinsing, draining, inspection and flat drying. Particularly useful for stabilising damaged field uniforms, rescue-training fabrics, flags, sample bags and heritage textiles without lifting them by weakened fibres. The inert, non-corroding mesh allows water and air to pass through while providing an even handling surface; it can be cut to fit trays or used as a sling between wash bath and drying rack. Each box contains one rolled sheet of white monofilament polyester support mesh, two reusable polyethylene securing clips, an archival pencil label and a care-and-cleaning guide. Rinse with deionised water before first use and clean between objects to avoid transferring silt or contaminants. Limitation: this mesh is a handling and drying support only; it does not remove mould, dyes, oils or chemical pollutants, and heavily degraded textiles should be assessed by a qualified conservator before wet treatment.

options.copy: Check wort and must sugar concentration quickly at home, beside a fermenter or while brewing away from mains power. Built for brewers who work outdoors, this compact optical refractometer has a rubber-armoured, splash-resistant body that is easy to grip with wet hands, plus automatic temperature compensation for typical Brisbane conditions. A few drops provide a clear Brix reading, helping you track mash extraction, estimate original gravity and follow fermentation without filling a hydrometer jar. The box includes the refractometer, padded hard case, daylight plate, calibration screwdriver, two sample pipettes, lens cloth, distilled-water calibration vial, Brix-to-specific-gravity reference card and instructions. Choose the scale that suits beer, cider, mead or higher-sugar ferments. Limitation: alcohol changes refractive readings after fermentation begins, so final gravity requires correction software or confirmation with a hydrometer; it is splash-resistant, not waterproof or submersible.

options.copy: Capture clear interviews, river-gauge maintenance notes and swift-water rescue training demonstrations for reports, videos and accurate subtitle transcription. Timecode support simplifies syncing footage from field cameras, and the compact charging case suits travel between remote monitoring sites. product_00064.name: Crewsaver Crewfit 165N Sport Automatic Inflatable Lifejacket

options.copy: A compact 165N automatic inflatable lifejacket for offshore boating, coastal gauge inspections and vessel-based fieldwork around Brisbane waterways. Its ergonomic 3D profile keeps movement unrestricted while checking telemetry, handling sampling equipment or boarding a workboat, and the automatic mechanism inflates after water immersion; a manual pull toggle and oral inflation tube provide backups. Reflective detailing, a whistle and an integrated lifting becket aid visibility and recovery during an emergency. In the box: one Crewfit 165N Sport lifejacket, fitted inflation cylinder and activation cartridge, whistle, crotch strap and user instructions. Limitation: this is not a specialist swift-water rescue PFD and should not be used for whitewater training, tethered rescue or repeated high-impact immersion; accidental activation is possible in very wet working conditions. The inflation system must be inspected before use and serviced after deployment or as specified by the manufacturer.

options.copy: Maintain access around river gauges, riparian monitoring sites and rescue-training areas without climbing or wading into avoidable hazards. Its removable hooked head helps pull free cut branches, while the high-visibility finish is easy to spot beside muddy banks and dense subtropical growth. Its sunlight-readable 3-inch colour display, multi-band GNSS support and preloaded TopoActive Australia and New Zealand maps help crews navigate riverbanks, access tracks and unfamiliar catchments. An IPX7 water rating, physical buttons and up to 165 hours of tracking battery life suit wet, gloved field use. The box contains the GPSMAP 67i, rechargeable lithium-ion battery pack, USB-C charging/data cable, carabiner clip and documentation. Limitation: satellite messaging, weather and SOS services require an active inReach subscription, and IPX7 protection covers temporary immersion only—the unit is not designed to float or serve as a marine distress beacon.

product_00070.name: RiverTrack Pro Handheld Acoustic Doppler Velocimeter Kit

options.copy: A rugged handheld acoustic Doppler velocimeter for measuring point velocity and calculating discharge in creeks, rivers and open channels. Designed for hydrology technicians working around Brisbane, it provides live velocity, depth and temperature readings, with Bluetooth logging to a phone or field tablet. The compact probe mounts to the supplied graduated wading rod, while IP67 electronics, high-visibility controls and a sunlight-readable display suit wet-season gauging and post-flood inspections. In the box: handheld display/logger, acoustic velocity probe with 3 m cable, two-piece 1.5 m graduated wading rod, mounting bracket, rechargeable battery, USB-C charger, Bluetooth data-export app licence, protective hard case, wrist lanyard and quick-start guide. Limitation: reliable readings require the probe to remain fully submerged in moving water; very shallow, highly aerated or debris-heavy flow can reduce accuracy, so it is not a substitute for a flood-rated remote gauge or safe swift-water procedures.

product_00071.name: River-Recovery Archival Textile Support Mesh Kit

options.copy: A conservation-grade support system for safely lifting, rinsing and air-drying waterlogged textiles after river work, equipment-store flooding or rescue-training exercises. The soft polyester mesh supports weakened fibres without trapping silt, while the rigid polypropylene frame keeps fabric flat and allows airflow from both sides. It is suited to fabric gauge-book covers, uniform insignia, training flags, webbing samples and other washable textile records exposed to mud or fresh water. Each box contains one reusable mesh support frame in the selected size, two removable polyester mesh sheets, eight non-corroding retaining clips, four frame feet, a soft sediment-lifting brush and a waterproof quick-reference treatment guide. All contact materials are uncoated, colourfast and suitable for repeated wet use. Limitation: this kit is not intended for drying rescue ropes, load-bearing harnesses, large garments or textiles with unstable dyes; contaminated, historically significant or chemically exposed items should be assessed by a qualified conservator.

options.copy: Measure the specific gravity of beer, cider, mead and other home ferments with a field-ready hydrometer kit designed for reliable readings after long days around water and equipment. The high-contrast scale helps you track fermentation progress, estimate alcohol content and confirm when a batch has stabilised, while the protective case makes the instrument easier to store in a work vehicle or brewing cupboard. The box includes one triple-scale glass hydrometer, a clear sampling tube with stable base, a food-grade sample thief, a temperature-correction chart, a cleaning brush and a padded protective case. product_00074.name: OceanGuard Pro 150N Manual Inflatable PFD with Safety Harness

options.copy: A low-profile Level 150 inflatable lifejacket for offshore vessel work, coastal gauge access and boat-based safety patrols. Its manual pull-tab inflation system helps avoid accidental deployment from rain, spray or repeated wet work, while the integrated stainless-steel harness and twin tether loops provide secure attachment on exposed decks. The fluorescent bladder includes reflective panels, a whistle, oral inflation tube and lifting becket for improved visibility and recovery. In the box: one OceanGuard Pro PFD, fitted 33 g CO₂ cylinder and manual firing head, crotch strap, safety whistle, inspection tag, storage bag and illustrated care guide. Available in two adult fits and high-visibility colours. Limitation: this is a manually activated offshore PFD and will not inflate automatically on immersion; it is not designed as a swift-water rescue vest and should not be used for training in fast-flowing rivers. The cylinder and firing mechanism require inspection after use and scheduled servicing.

product_00075.name: RiverReach Telescopic Arborist Pole Saw Kit

options.copy: Trim overhanging branches and light woody growth around river gauges, access tracks and rescue-training sites while keeping both feet on the ground. The oval aluminium shaft provides a secure grip in humid Brisbane conditions, telescopes without loose sections and packs down for transport in a field vehicle. A curved 390 mm impulse-hardened blade cuts efficiently on the pull stroke, while the branch hook helps dislodge small cut limbs from instrument enclosures or walkways. In the box: telescopic pole assembly, replaceable pruning blade, blade guard, branch-hook head, shoulder carry bag, hex key and care guide. Rinse and dry the blade and locking collars after exposure to muddy or brackish water. Limitation: this is a manual pruning tool for branches up to 100 mm diameter and is not insulated, so it must not be used near powerlines or from boats, ladders or unstable banks.

options.copy: A rugged clinical reference for swift-water rescue training, river-gauge fieldwork and other wet or remote operations. The wipe-clean, waterproof guide provides concise prompts for primary assessment, drowning response, hypothermia, heat illness, spinal precautions, bleeding control, envenomation, crush injury and structured handover to Queensland Ambulance Service. Colour-coded tabs and high-contrast flowcharts are designed for quick consultation in rain, spray or low light, while Australian terminology and emergency numbers suit local teams. This guide is a memory aid only: it does not replace accredited first-aid or rescue training, local operating procedures, clinical judgement or current Australian Resuscitation Council guidance.

options.copy: A compact emergency beacon for offshore passages, remote river-gauge inspections and swift-water rescue training where mobile coverage cannot be relied upon. The buoyant, waterproof housing has glove-friendly controls, an antenna deployment guide and a sealed long-life battery, while the supplied pouch secures to a PFD or equipment belt. In the box: RescueLink beacon with battery installed, protective flotation pouch, retaining lanyard, belt/PFD attachment strap, registration instructions, self-test guide and quick-reference card. Limitation: this is a one-way distress device and cannot send messages or confirm that rescuers are responding; Australian registration is required and activation is for genuine emergencies only.

options.copy: A waterproof, field-ready clinical reference for first responders assessing and managing immersion incidents, drowning, hypothermia, floodwater exposure and common river-rescue injuries. Designed for swift-water trainers and remote field crews, it uses concise flowcharts, observation prompts and Australian terminology to support handovers, training scenarios and decisions while awaiting ambulance care. Mud-resistant synthetic pages can be wiped clean, while rounded corners and a tether eyelet suit use beside gauges, in rescue boats or at wet training sites. In the box: one spiral-bound quick-reference guide, one casualty assessment card, one hypothermia staging card, one waterproof pencil and one detachable lanyard. Limitation: this guide is an educational reference only; it does not replace accredited clinical training, local Queensland Ambulance Service protocols, medical direction or emergency services. Always call Triple Zero (000) for serious incidents.

options.copy: Built for gauge runs, small-boat navigation and swift-water rescue training, the AquaNav R1 is a buoyant handheld GPS designed for wet, fast-moving environments. Its glove-friendly controls, sunlight-readable 3.2-inch display and high-sensitivity multi-GNSS receiver help crews mark river gauges, boat ramps, hazards, access tracks and training locations. Australian topographic and inland-waterway mapping is preloaded, while track recording and waypoint averaging support repeat field visits. An IPX7-rated housing, high-visibility shell and integrated strobe make recovery easier if the unit is dropped overboard. In the box: AquaNav R1 GPS, rechargeable battery, USB-C charging cable, wrist lanyard, belt clip, quick-start guide and one-year Australian warranty. Limitation: it has no satellite messaging or emergency beacon function, and IPX7 protection covers temporary immersion to 1 metre rather than prolonged submersion; always carry approved communications and navigation backups.

Mud-resistant synthetic pages can be wiped clean, while rounded corners and a stainless-steel split ring suit a rescue vest, vehicle kit or field pack. In the box: one double-sided reference booklet, one detachable casualty-assessment card, a permanent marking pencil and a split-ring attachment. This is a prompt aid only; it does not replace accredited clinical training, local water-authority procedures, current Australian Resuscitation Council guidance or direction from ambulance clinicians.

product_00099.name: Garmin GPSMAP 79s Floating Handheld Marine GPS

options.copy: Built for boat crews, river-gauge technicians and swift-water rescue teams, the GPSMAP 79s provides reliable position, track and waypoint navigation in a rugged, water-resistant handheld that floats if dropped overboard. Its high-contrast colour display remains readable in bright Queensland sun, while physical buttons can be operated with wet or gloved hands. Use it to mark gauge sites, boat ramps, hazards and rescue access points, record survey tracks, or navigate back to a launch location in poor visibility. Multi-band GNSS support improves positioning around steep banks and tree cover, and wireless connectivity allows compatible waypoint and track sharing. In the box are the GPSMAP 79s handheld, USB charging/data cable, wrist lanyard and documentation. Two user-replaceable AA batteries are required and are not included. Limitation: the supplied worldwide basemap is suitable for general orientation only; detailed Australian marine charts must be purchased and loaded separately.

Limitation: this contact meter records a manual spot reading only; it does not log changing levels or transmit telemetry, and turbulent, highly conductive or contaminated water may make the exact contact point harder to identify.

product_00109.name: RiverTrack R7 Rugged Handheld Marine GPS Navigator

options.copy: Built for river-gauge servicing, small-boat navigation and swift-water rescue training, the RiverTrack R7 provides reliable position, track, speed and waypoint data on a sunlight-readable 3.5-inch colour display. Its glove-friendly controls, high-visibility housing, IP67 water resistance and buoyant design suit wet fieldwork around Brisbane’s rivers, creeks and boat ramps. Preloaded Australian coastal and inland-water basemaps help crews mark gauge sites, access points, hazards and rescue staging areas, while GPS and Galileo reception supports tracking in steep or tree-lined reaches. The unit records routes and can share GPX files with compatible computers via USB. In the box are the R7 navigator, rechargeable lithium battery, USB-C charging/data cable, wrist lanyard, belt clip, quick-start guide and screen protector. Limitation: detailed marine charts, live depth data and emergency satellite messaging are not included and require separate compatible services or equipment.

options.copy: A rugged portable current meter for measuring point velocity in rivers, creeks, culverts and open channels. Designed for routine gauge-station visits, discharge measurements and training-site assessments, its streamlined propeller sensor mounts to a wading rod and sends live speed, average velocity and sample count to the splash-resistant handheld display. The backlit screen and large controls are practical for wet-weather work, while internal logging stores readings for later entry into field records. In the box: handheld display, velocity sensor, selected-length sensor cable, three-section 1.5 m graduated wading rod, spare propeller, USB data lead, wrist lanyard, calibration certificate, quick-start guide and padded carry case. Limitation: the propeller requires adequate depth and relatively clean flow; weeds, heavy sediment, debris or very shallow water can foul the rotor and reduce accuracy, so it is not suitable for unattended flood deployment.

product_00111.name: RiverSafe Archival Textile Drying Mesh Kit

options.copy: A conservation-grade drying support for stabilising waterlogged uniforms, fabric equipment labels, historic flood-response textiles and other flat or lightly shaped items after rinsing. Well suited to a hydrology workshop or rescue-training store, the inert polyester mesh promotes airflow while supporting wet fibres, and the modular frame keeps material away from contaminated benches during documentation and controlled drying. The smooth mesh can also be placed beneath fragile textiles during low-suction surface cleaning. The box contains one snap-together polypropylene frame, one removable white polyester mesh panel, four corner clips, eight textile-safe retaining tabs and an archival pencil identification tag. Components can be rinsed and reused between jobs. Limitation: this kit is intended for air drying small, structurally sound textiles only; it must not be used to lift heavy saturated garments, support people, or dry objects contaminated by sewage, fuel or unknown river pollutants without specialist assessment.

Its water-resistant, rubber-armoured body and lanyard suit field-oriented brewers who want dependable equipment that packs neatly into a work bag or home-brew kit. Limitation: once fermentation has begun, alcohol affects refractometer results, so final-gravity readings require a correction calculator or confirmation with a hydrometer; the unit must not be submerged.

options.copy: A compact 406 MHz personal locator beacon for offshore crews, river-gauge field teams and swift-water rescuers who need a last-resort distress signal beyond mobile coverage. Its one-handed controls, buoyant pouch and seven-year battery life suit grab bags, PFD pockets and remote field kits. options.copy: Built for river-gauge inspections, boat approaches and swift-water rescue training, the RiverTrack Pro is a rugged handheld marine GPS for recording waypoints, following tracks and navigating back to access points in rain, spray and muddy field conditions. High-contrast controls can be operated with wet gloves, while the sunlight-readable screen shows position, speed, heading, distance and breadcrumb trails. IPX7 water resistance, a buoyant high-visibility housing and replaceable AA batteries suit long shifts around Brisbane’s rivers, creeks and flood-prone crossings. The 32 GB and 64 GB versions provide storage for maps, routes and field waypoints. In the box are the GPS navigator, removable wrist lanyard, USB-C data cable, rail/boat cradle, two AA lithium batteries, screen protector and quick-start guide. Limitation: this unit is a navigation aid only; it does not replace official marine charts, local flood intelligence or rescue risk assessment, and satellite reception may be reduced beneath bridges, dense canopy or steep banks.

options.copy: A rugged electric contact meter for measuring water depth and static level in monitoring wells, stilling wells and gauge installations. Designed for routine river-station maintenance around South East Queensland, it uses a stainless-steel probe, high-visibility millimetre-marked tape and bright light-and-buzzer indication when the probe reaches water. The IP67 reel electronics, brake-equipped frame and replaceable probe make it practical for wet fieldwork, while the metric graduations support repeatable gauge checks and datum records. In the box: RiverTrack Pro reel with selected tape length, 16 mm water-sensing probe, protective probe holder, four AA batteries, cleaning brush, field calibration certificate, quick-start guide and padded carry case. Limitation: this contact instrument measures a single water level only; it does not log readings or measure flow velocity, and conductive foam or heavily contaminated water may trigger an early indication.

options.copy: Stabilise waterlogged uniforms, rescue-training textiles, fabric equipment tags and small heritage cloth items after river exposure or storm damage. These conservation-grade, acid-free cotton blotters draw moisture and suspended grime from rinsed textiles during flat drying, helping reduce tide marks, dye transfer and distortion. They are suitable for use at a gauge depot, incident staging area or conservation workbench, and can be cut to fit around seams, patches and reflective tape. Each box contains 25 white blotter sheets in the selected size, 10 sheets of inert polyester release film to prevent sticking, 20 interleaving tissue sheets, a reusable polyethylene storage sleeve and a concise wet-textile handling guide. Replace blotters as they become saturated and allow airflow around the object. Limitation: this pack does not disinfect sewage-contaminated material and is not suitable for actively moulding, structurally fragile or colour-bleeding textiles without assessment by a qualified conservator.

options.copy: Brew reliable beer, cider or hard ginger beer around an outdoor work roster with this lightweight, pressure-rated fermenter. Its clear PET body makes fermentation easy to check before or after a day servicing river gauges, while the compact footprint suits a Brisbane garage, utility room or shaded training shed. Pressure capability allows closed transfers and natural carbonation with less exposure to oxygen, and the wide opening simplifies cleaning after each batch. The box includes one pressure-rated PET fermenter, screw-on lid, pressure-release valve, carbonation caps, floating dip tube with filter, stick-on temperature strip, bottling tap, sediment collector, seals and an illustrated setup guide. Capacity choices cover small trial batches through to club-sized brews. Limitation: the vessel is not suitable for hot-fill use; wort must be cooled below 35°C before transfer, and active fermentation should be kept out of direct Queensland sun.

product_00123.name: RiverCom Rugged Wireless Field Audio Kit

options.copy: Capture clear spoken notes during river-gauge inspections, safety briefings and swift-water rescue training without keeping a phone or camera close to the speaker. The compact wireless microphone records a backup track internally while transmitting audio to the weather-sealed receiver, helping preserve commentary around rushing water, pumps and road noise. A high-visibility windscreen and locking lapel clip suit exposed riverbanks, boats and training sites, while USB-C charging makes the kit easy to replenish from a vehicle power bank. In the box: wireless transmitter microphone, camera/phone receiver, lavalier microphone, high-visibility foam windscreen, furry wind cover, locking clip, USB-C charging cable, 3.5 mm camera lead, USB-C phone adaptor, Lightning phone adaptor and padded carry case. Limitation: the transmitter tolerates rain and splashes but is not submersible, so it must not be worn during in-water rescue exercises.

options.copy: A compact personal locator beacon for offshore passages, remote river-gauge inspections and swift-water rescue training where mobile coverage cannot be trusted. When activated, the waterproof unit transmits a 406 MHz distress alert with GPS position through the international Cospas-Sarsat satellite network, while a 121.5 MHz homing signal and high-intensity strobe help search crews locate the wearer. Its glove-friendly controls, buoyant body and PFD attachment clip suit wet, fast-moving environments around Brisbane and Moreton Bay. In the box: RescueLink 406 GPS beacon with sealed long-life battery, PFD/belt mounting clip, wrist lanyard, reflective identification label, Australian registration instructions and user guide. Limitation: this is an emergency distress device only; it does not provide two-way messaging or confirm that rescuers have received the alert, and it must be registered to the owner before use.

options.copy: Clear overhanging branches around river gauges, access tracks and rescue-training sites from the ground with the RiverReach Telescopic Arborist Pole Saw. Designed for riparian maintenance, its oval aluminium shaft offers a secure grip in wet Brisbane conditions, while the impulse-hardened curved blade cuts green limbs cleanly and a hooked tip helps control small branches. A quick-lock extension system packs down for transport in a field vehicle or equipment boat, and the replaceable blade and corrosion-resistant fittings simplify ongoing maintenance. In the box: one telescopic pole assembly, one 390 mm pruning-saw blade, one branch hook, one blade guard, one shoulder carry strap, a hex key and an instruction guide. Choose the reach that suits routine gauge access or taller vegetation. Limitation: this is a ground-operated pruning tool only; it is not insulated for work near powerlines and should not be used to cut branches thicker than 150 mm or while standing in moving water.

options.copy: Keep gauge components, water-sampling kits, throw bags and wet PPE clearly identified while moving between depots, vehicles and river sites. These tear-resistant synthetic tags accept permanent marker and feature a reinforced eyelet with a locking cable tie, making them useful for recording asset numbers, site names, inspection dates or contamination status. The bright orange surface remains easy to spot inside dark equipment cases, while the writable white panel provides space for operational notes. Each box contains 100 waterproof tags and 100 black 200 mm locking cable ties, packed in a resealable dispenser carton for the workshop or response vehicle. Choose the tag size to suit anything from instrument cases to bundled rescue gear. Limitation: the writing is water resistant only when applied with a suitable permanent industrial marker; ordinary pens may smear or wash off, and the tags are not intended to replace certified dangerous-goods labels.
